EdgeCase comes with a collection of real networks. They range from classic examples of a few dozen
nodes, small enough to draw and reason about by eye, to networks with hundreds of thousands of edges
that are useful for checking how an analysis scales. Each loads with a single function call and
needs no network connection, except for three very large graphs that are downloaded on first use.

## Loading a dataset

Every dataset has its own loader function, which returns a `Graph`:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec

florentine = ec.florentine_families()
florentine
```

The loaded graph is an ordinary `Graph`, with a name, labels, and any attributes the data includes.
It can be analyzed, modified, and drawn like any other graph, and each call to the loader returns a
fresh copy, so changes never carry over from one use to the next.

## The classic networks

These small networks appear throughout the network science literature, and each has become the
standard example of some idea. Their nodes carry the names or attributes of the original data.

| Loader | Nodes | Edges | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`karate_club()`](../reference/karate_club.qmd) | 34 | 78 | Friendships among the members of a university karate club that split in two. Node attributes `faction` and `role`. |
| [`florentine_families()`](../reference/florentine_families.qmd) | 15 | 20 | Marriage ties among the leading families of Renaissance Florence, labelled by family name. |
| [`les_miserables()`](../reference/les_miserables.qmd) | 77 | 254 | Characters of Victor Hugo's novel, joined when they appear in the same chapter. Weighted by the number of shared chapters. |
| [`davis_southern_women()`](../reference/davis_southern_women.qmd) | 32 | 89 | Eighteen women and the fourteen social events they attended. Bipartite, with a `bipartite` attribute of `0` for women and `1` for events. |

The Florentine families are the textbook case for betweenness centrality. The Medici were neither
the wealthiest nor the most powerful family in Florence, but they married into families that had
no ties to one another, and so sat on most of the shortest paths through the network:

```{python}
(
    florentine.betweenness_centrality()
    .get_node_df()
    .sort("betweenness_centrality", descending=True)
    .head(4)
)
```

The Medici's betweenness is double that of the next family, which is the network's account of how
they rose to dominate the city.

*Les Misérables* is weighted, and its communities match the novel's storylines. The weighted
Louvain method finds them, and drawing the graph by community shows Valjean at the center, linked
to almost everyone, with Myriel and his small circle of minor characters off to one side:

```{python}
les_mis = ec.les_miserables().cmty_louvain()
les_mis.plot(color_by="cmty_louvain", size_by="degree", show_labels=False, seed=2)
```

The Southern Women data is the standard example of a *two-mode* network, in which edges only join
nodes of different kinds. Projecting it onto the women gives a one-mode network in which two women
are linked when they attended an event together, weighted by the number of events they shared:

```{python}
women = ec.davis_southern_women().bipartite_projection(which=0)
women.get_edge_df().sort("weight", descending=True).head(3)
```

Evelyn Jefferson (ID 1) and Theresa Anderson (ID 3) attended seven events together, more than any
other pair. [Network biology](network-biology.qmd) and the reference page for
[`bipartite_projection()`](../reference/Graph.bipartite_projection.qmd) have more on two-mode
networks.

## Networks from data repositories

The remaining datasets come from two widely used public collections, the
[Stanford Large Network Dataset Collection](https://snap.stanford.edu/data/) (SNAP) and
[Network Repository](https://networkrepository.com). They are distributed as edge lists, so their
nodes have no attributes, and each node is labelled with its number in the original file.

| Loader | Nodes | Edges | Directed | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [`dolphins()`](../reference/dolphins.qmd) | 62 | 159 | no | Frequent associations among bottlenose dolphins in Doubtful Sound, New Zealand |
| [`football()`](../reference/football.qmd) | 35 | 119 | no | Games between American college football teams |
| [`polbooks()`](../reference/polbooks.qmd) | 105 | 441 | no | Books about US politics frequently bought together on Amazon |
| [`jazz()`](../reference/jazz.qmd) | 198 | 2,743 | no | Collaborations among jazz musicians |
| [`celegans()`](../reference/celegans.qmd) | 453 | 2,041 | no | The metabolic network of the nematode *C. elegans* |
| [`power_grid()`](../reference/power_grid.qmd) | 4,941 | 6,594 | no | The power grid of the western United States |
| [`ca_grqc()`](../reference/ca_grqc.qmd) | 5,242 | 28,980 | no | Co-authorships in the general relativity section of arXiv |
| [`internet()`](../reference/internet.qmd) | 6,474 | 13,895 | no | Links between autonomous systems of the Internet, January 2000 |
| [`gnutella()`](../reference/gnutella.qmd) | 6,301 | 20,777 | yes | A snapshot of the Gnutella peer-to-peer network, August 2002 |
| [`wiki_vote()`](../reference/wiki_vote.qmd) | 7,115 | 103,689 | yes | Votes in Wikipedia administrator elections |
| [`pgp()`](../reference/pgp.qmd) | 10,680 | 24,340 | yes | The PGP web of trust |
| [`physics()`](../reference/physics.qmd) | 12,008 | 237,010 | no | Co-authorships in the high energy physics (phenomenology) section of arXiv |
| [`condmat()`](../reference/condmat.qmd) | 23,133 | 186,936 | no | Co-authorships in the condensed matter section of arXiv |
| [`enron()`](../reference/enron.qmd) | 36,692 | 367,662 | yes | Email between Enron employees |

All of these are shipped with EdgeCase in compressed form and load in at most a second or two. The
larger ones are good for seeing how an algorithm behaves on a realistic, sparse network. The power
grid, for example, is a *large-world* network. A grid spread across half a continent has few
shortcuts, so its diameter and mean distance are long:

```{python}
grid = ec.power_grid()
grid.diameter(), round(grid.mean_distance(), 2)
```

The farthest pair of nodes is 46 links apart and a typical pair about 19. Those distances are long
for a network of under 5,000 nodes: the karate club and most other small social networks have mean
distances of 2 to 3, and even the co-authorship networks, with thousands of authors, stay around 6.

Because these nodes are labelled with numbers stored as strings, the usual rule about IDs and labels
applies with full force: `grid.get_node(1)` is the node with ID 1, while `grid.get_node("1")` is the
node that was numbered 1 in the source file. See [The graph model](graph-model.qmd#referring-to-nodes).

The files are loaded as published, which means that some of these graphs aren't simple. The three
co-authorship networks (`ca_grqc()`, `physics()`, and `condmat()`) list every collaboration in both
directions, so each undirected edge appears twice, and a few datasets, notably `internet()`,
contain self-loops. Their edge counts above include the duplicates. Measures such as degree and
node-level clustering count every edge, so for most analyses it is best to
[`simplify()`](../reference/Graph.simplify.qmd) these graphs first:

```{python}
coauthors = ec.ca_grqc()
coauthors.is_simple(), coauthors.simplify().count_edges()
```

Once simplified, the general relativity network has 14,484 distinct collaborations.

## Very large networks

Three registered datasets are too large to ship with the package:

| Name | Nodes | Edges | Directed | Download |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `web_google` ([`web_google()`](../reference/web_google.qmd)) | 875,713 | 5,105,039 | yes | 10 MB |
| `roadnet_pa` | 1,087,562 | 1,541,514 | no | 5 MB |
| `soc_livejournal` ([`soc_livejournal()`](../reference/soc_livejournal.qmd)) | 4,847,571 | 68,993,773 | yes | 120 MB |

The first call downloads the data and stores it in `~/.cache/edgecase/datasets/`, and later calls
read it from there. Set the environment variable `EDGECASE_NO_DOWNLOAD=1` to turn downloading off,
for example on a machine without network access; loading a dataset that isn't on disk then raises a
`FileNotFoundError` instead.

```python
web = ec.web_google()   # downloads about 10 MB the first time
```

## The dataset registry

The loaders are convenient wrappers around a registry of datasets, which can also be used directly.
[`list_registered_datasets()`](../reference/list_registered_datasets.qmd) gives the names of the
registered datasets:

```{python}
ec.list_registered_datasets()
```

Most names match their loader functions. The exceptions are `karate` (`karate_club()`), `ca_hepph`
(`physics()`), and `ca_condmat` (`condmat()`).

[`get_dataset_info()`](../reference/get_dataset_info.qmd) returns a dataset's metadata without
loading it, including its size, source, and whether it is bundled or downloaded:

```{python}
ec.get_dataset_info("jazz")
```

and [`load_dataset()`](../reference/load_dataset.qmd) loads a dataset by name. Its `directed=`
argument overrides the registry's setting, which is a way to load a directed network as an
undirected one, and `weighted=True` keeps the weights of a weighted file:

```{python}
ec.load_dataset("wiki_vote", directed=False).is_directed()
```

The registry holds only the networks distributed as data files, so the four classic networks with
attributes are available only through their own loaders. `load_dataset("karate")` loads the same
friendships as `karate_club()`, but without the `faction` and `role` attributes.

Datasets are stored in the Matrix Market format, and
[`list_available_datasets()`](../reference/list_available_datasets.qmd) lists the files found on
disk. To load your own Matrix Market files, use
[`from_matrix_market()`](../reference/from_matrix_market.qmd), described in
[File formats](file-formats.qmd).

## Choosing a dataset

For learning a method or checking that it behaves as expected, start with a classic network whose
answer is known: the karate club for communities, the Florentine families for centrality, the
Southern Women for bipartite methods, and *Les Misérables* for anything weighted. Move to the
repository networks to see how a method copes with a larger, messier graph, and to
[generators](generators.qmd) when you need a graph whose structure you control exactly.
